strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically important question: whether internal signals can monitor generalization during large-scale, one-pass LLM pretraining without repeatedly running downstream evaluations.
Analyzing public checkpoints of a 7B MoE model across math, code, commonsense, and scientific QA is more realistic than the small synthetic settings predominant in earlier grokking work.
The proposed routing statistics are intuitive, and comparing them with training and validation loss is a potentially useful empirical direction.
The paper attempts several complementary analyses, including layerwise routing dynamics, parameter-update dynamics, contamination filtering, and a theoretical connection to routing-kernel complexity.
weaknesses: The central evidence for delayed generalization is circular. The analysis retains test examples whose predictions become consistently correct by the end of pretraining and groups them by the checkpoint at which this happens. Consequently, their eventual accuracy and apparent rise are built into the selection and grouping procedure. Training examples are analogously grouped by their first stable-loss checkpoint, after which the two post-hoc groups are semantically matched. This does not establish a causal memorization-to-generalization lag or grokking.

The notion of memorization is not adequately justified for one-pass pretraining. Low NLL on samples drawn from the pretraining corpus can occur before those samples are encountered and may represent ordinary distributional generalization rather than memorization. The criterion also uses the final checkpoint loss, leaking future trajectory information into the group definition; no audit of each sample's actual exposure position is provided.

Downstream performance is confounded by separately LoRA-tuning every checkpoint. No repeated tuning runs, random-seed variability, error bars, or direct evaluation controls are reported, so changes in adaptation behavior may explain part of the trajectory. Important details such as prompts, decoding, optimizer, schedule, splits, and retained sample counts are missing. The claim of 10,000 test examples per domain is also inconsistent with benchmarks such as HumanEvalPlus and the MMLU college-chemistry subset, which contain far fewer unique problems.

The correlation analysis is strongly biased: it includes only checkpoints after accuracy has begun a sustained rise, uses very few temporally ordered observations, and correlates quantities that all trend with training time. There is no detrending, time-matched control, held-out trajectory, prospective prediction experiment, or evaluation on another model. Thus correlations near 0.9 do not demonstrate a reliable monitor or mechanism.

The pathway-consistency definition contradicts its interpretation. The stated quantity is one minus a normalized cosine similarity, and the paper explicitly says higher values indicate more erratic routing, yet increasing values and positive accuracy correlations are described as improved consistency and smoother routing. Figure 7 also appears to swap the two metric labels: the approximately 0.3 range corresponds to consistency in earlier figures, whereas the approximately 680 range corresponds to edit distance. These inconsistencies undermine the principal empirical result.

The edit-distance metric is under-specified and fragile. Its expert-weight threshold is never given, pathways are described as delimiter-separated strings without clarifying token-level versus character-level Levenshtein distance, and no normalization or sensitivity analysis is supplied. Varying route lengths and multi-digit expert identifiers can distort the measure. Pairwise computation over 10,000 samples is also quadratic, contradicting the claim of essentially zero cost.

The theoretical result does not support the empirical claims. It assumes fixed routing in a one-layer NTK model, whereas the claimed mechanism is dynamically evolving routing in a multilayer pretrained MoE. The proof contains dimensional inconsistencies in the ridge-regression solution, equates out-of-sample variance with a training-Gram trace without sufficient assumptions, and gives an incorrect concentration scaling for averaged squared Gaussian noise. No theorem relates edit distance to effective dimension; only an incompletely specified synthetic correlation is presented.

The experimental scope is insufficient for the broad claims: only one model and ten checkpoints are studied, with no other MoE architecture, model size, training run, or routing baseline such as router entropy, load balance, routing overlap, or representation similarity. The arbitrary removal of the top 10% by Min-K%++ is uncalibrated and cannot ensure that remaining benchmark examples were unseen. Threshold ablations for memorization, stability, routing selection, and contamination are absent, and neither code nor a complete reproducibility specification is provided. These issues make the central claims unsupported rather than merely incomplete.

weaknesses: The central grokking claim is not established. Low loss on an earlier training example does not distinguish memorization from ordinary generalization, while continued pretraining supplies substantial new, potentially relevant data. Moreover, test groups are defined by eventual persistent correctness, only eventually successful examples are emphasized, and training/test groups are matched post hoc. These choices largely construct the delayed curves rather than demonstrate a memorization-caused generalization transition.

The proposed monitor is acausal and test-leaky: identifying a memorized sample requires its final-checkpoint loss and all future checkpoints, while the correlation window is selected using the point at which test accuracy begins its sustained rise. Thus the reported procedure cannot support the claimed real-time, evaluation-free monitoring use case.

The correlations use at most ten temporally ordered checkpoints—and apparently only about five in parts of the nanoMoE analysis. Monotonic change with training time, serial dependence, outcome-based window selection, and absent repeated seeds can readily produce extreme correlations. There is no time-controlled baseline, prospective prediction experiment, confidence interval, or held-out calibration across trajectories.

The pathway-consistency result is internally contradictory. The definition explicitly says larger C means more erratic and less consistent routing, yet C increases in Figure 6 and correlates positively with accuracy, which the paper interprets as increased consistency. Figure 7 also appears to swap the metric labels: the purported distance plot has the approximately 0.3 scale of C, whereas the purported consistency plot has the hundreds-scale of edit distance.

The theoretical result does not justify the empirical mechanism. It assumes a one-layer model with a fixed router, whereas the empirical claim concerns evolving routers in a multilayer MoE. The proof is dimensionally inconsistent in its primal/dual kernel expressions, adds irreducible noise to risk against the noiseless target, uses an unjustified variance identity and concentration rate, and asserts O(1/n) decay without sufficient spectral or target assumptions. Lower effective dimension can also increase bias. No theorem connects pathway edit distance or consistency to the bound; the synthetic experiment only correlates random-router edit distance with effective dimension, not generalization.

Experimental support is too narrow for the broad claims: the main evidence comes from one pretrained-model trajectory, the nanoMoE replication is one incompletely specified run, and separately LoRA-tuning every checkpoint introduces uncontrolled optimization variance. Baselines are mostly training/validation loss; comparisons with checkpoint index, router norms, entropy as a predictor, representation similarity, effective rank, and other internal progress measures are missing.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The claimed 10,000 test examples per domain conflicts with the sizes of listed benchmarks such as HumanEval+ and MMLU college chemistry. Actual split sizes, prompts, decoding and scoring details, per-domain epsilon values, analyzed checkpoint subsets, group sizes, matching quality, random seeds, and nanoMoE architecture/training configuration are missing, and no code or artifact link is provided.

Claims such as “zero cost,” “faithfully track,” and contamination-free evaluation are overstated. Pairwise edit distance over thousands of samples is quadratic and requires routing instrumentation, while removing the top 10% by an uncalibrated membership score cannot ensure that all remaining benchmark examples are unseen.

Moreover, domain-specific loss thresholds are selected to force 20–25% of samples to qualify before the final checkpoint, and the criterion explicitly uses final-checkpoint loss. Thus the claimed ordering from memorization to generalization is not convincingly established.

The monitoring claim relies on correlations among mostly monotonic quantities over only ten checkpoints, further restricted to checkpoints after accuracy begins its sustained rise. There is no control for training step, detrending, prospective prediction, held-out calibration, seed-level uncertainty, or comparison to generic time-dependent model statistics. The near-perfect correlations therefore do not demonstrate that the metrics independently predict generalization.

The pathway-consistency definition is internally contradictory: the equation and accompanying text state that larger values mean more erratic, less consistent transitions, whereas the figures and correlation analysis interpret increasing values as improved consistency and better generalization. The edit-distance metric is also underspecified regarding token-level versus character-level edits and is sensitive to pathway length, thresholding, and expert-index representation.

weaknesses: The central grokking evidence is largely circular. Training groups are defined by when loss becomes stably low, while test groups are defined by when predictions become stably correct; plotting these selected groups necessarily produces a loss plateau followed by an accuracy transition. Post-hoc Hungarian matching between these groups does not establish that memorizing particular training samples causes delayed generalization.

Low, stable next-token loss is not evidence that a sample has been memorized, especially in near-single-pass training where low loss may reflect ordinary distributional generalization. The domain-specific loss thresholds are explicitly selected to force 20–25% of samples to count as memorized, and the criterion depends on the final checkpoint and all future checkpoints. This undermines both the grokking interpretation and the claimed online-monitoring use case.

The correlation results are vulnerable to severe time confounding: routing metrics and accuracy are both smooth functions of training step, correlations are computed only after accuracy begins its sustained rise, and apparently very few checkpoints remain. There is no detrending, partial correlation against training step, prospective prediction, held-out trajectory, or comparison with other time-dependent internal statistics. Consequently, high Pearson/Spearman correlations do not demonstrate a reliable monitor.

The pathway-consistency metric is internally contradictory. Its formula is one minus normalized cosine similarity, and the text explicitly says higher values indicate more erratic routing, yet increasing values are repeatedly interpreted as smoother, more consistent pathways and assigned a preferred positive correlation with accuracy. Moreover, cosine similarity between independently parameterized router rows in different layers lacks a demonstrated invariant or functional meaning.

The edit-distance metric is insufficiently justified: it applies Levenshtein distance to variable-length strings of expert indices and delimiters, can conflate multi-digit identifiers and layer alignment, and treats layer-local expert identities as directly comparable. The reported trends could reflect changes in routing concentration, sequence composition, or expert utilization rather than shared computational mechanisms; the limited entropy and cross-domain checks do not rule these alternatives out.

The theoretical result is not sound as presented. The ridge-regression derivation contains dimensionally inconsistent expressions, moves between centered and uncentered labels, adds irreducible label noise while bounding error to the noiseless target, and does not justify replacing population feature covariance with the empirical Gram matrix. The claimed O(1/n) decay does not follow without additional spectral and target assumptions. Lower effective dimension can also increase bias, so it does not by itself imply an improved bound.

The theory analyzes a one-layer MoE with a fixed router, whereas the empirical claim concerns evolving multilayer routing and cross-layer consistency. The synthetic correlation between edit distance and effective dimension neither validates the real-model metrics nor demonstrates improved predictive generalization.

The downstream evaluation is poorly controlled. Each checkpoint undergoes separate three-epoch LoRA tuning without repeated seeds or uncertainty estimates, so changing accuracy may reflect finetuning variability or checkpoint-specific adaptability. The claim of 10,000 test examples per domain also conflicts with the stated benchmarks, including HumanEval+ and the MMLU college-chemistry subset, which are far smaller.

Only ten checkpoints are used to infer sharp transitions, group sizes and raw benchmark results are not adequately reported, and essential prompt, decoding, sampling, and reproducibility details are missing. Overall, the main claims of grokking, mechanistic explanation, and evaluation-free monitoring are substantially stronger than the evidence.

strengths: The paper studies an important and underexplored question: whether useful generalization signals can be obtained from internal dynamics during large-scale pretraining.
Using public OLMoE checkpoints across four domains is valuable, and the additional nanoMoE experiment attempts to test whether the observations persist across model scales.
The proposed routing statistics are intuitive at a high level, and the paper compares them with training and validation loss while providing several sensitivity analyses.
The manuscript is generally readable and motivates the practical relevance of pretraining-time monitoring clearly.
weaknesses: The central grokking evidence is circular and post hoc. The memorization threshold is chosen to force 20–25% of samples to qualify; test samples are selected using their future correctness and grouped by the checkpoint after which they remain correct. Consequently, the performance jumps in Figures 1–2 largely follow by construction. Embedding-based matching performed after these groups are defined does not establish a temporal or causal link between particular training examples and generalization.

The interpretation as grokking is not justified in a continually changing, near-single-pass data stream. Low NLL on a training example does not by itself demonstrate memorization, and later improvement can arise from subsequently encountered related data. No intervention, data-order control, or matched unseen-data comparison separates delayed generalization from ordinary continued learning.

The monitoring correlations are computed on only ten checkpoints and further restricted to a target-dependent interval beginning after accuracy starts its sustained rise. Smooth metrics and accuracy naturally correlate through training time and autocorrelation; there is no detrending, prospective prediction, held-out calibration, independent OLMoE run, or causal perturbation. Fine-tuning every checkpoint without seeds or uncertainty estimates adds another major confound. Moreover, identifying the analyzed samples requires the final checkpoint, so the method as evaluated is not a real-time monitor.

The pathway-distance metric applies character-level Levenshtein distance to serialized decimal expert IDs. It is sensitive to arbitrary expert numbering, delimiters, the number of digits in an ID, and pathway length, and can align across layer boundaries. It is therefore not a principled or permutation-invariant measure of computational similarity. Averaging routes over all tokens also discards substantial routing structure.

The second metric is internally contradictory. Its formula is one minus normalized cosine similarity, and the text explicitly says larger values indicate more erratic transitions, yet increasing values are called greater consistency and interpreted as smoother routing. The reported positive accuracy correlations therefore support the opposite of the claimed mechanism. Figure 7 also appears to swap the numerical ranges and labels of the two pathway metrics.

The theoretical section does not validate the empirical claims. It analyzes a one-layer model with a frozen router, unlike the evolving multilayer routing under study. The purported bound lacks necessary distributional and boundedness assumptions, contains dimensionally inconsistent ridge-regression algebra, conflates excess risk to the noiseless target with label-noise risk, and gives an unsupported test-variance expression and O(1/n) claim. A synthetic correlation between edit distance and effective dimension under random frozen routers neither proves that edit distance controls effective dimension nor that either causes generalization in OLMoE.

Evaluation and reproducibility details are inconsistent or missing. The paper claims 10,000 test examples per domain even though HumanEvalPlus and MMLU college chemistry are far smaller, without explaining resampling or the actual evaluation sets. Removing the top 10% by an uncalibrated Min-K%++ score cannot ensure that the remainder is uncontaminated. Raw benchmark accuracies, prompts, decoding settings, repeated-run variability, and multiple-testing corrections are absent. The nanoMoE footnote is empty, and its architecture, optimizer, routing configuration, seeds, checkpoints, and released code/model are not specified.

Overall, the interesting observational premise does not overcome the circular construction of the main phenomenon, invalid interpretation of one metric, confounded correlation analysis, and technically unsound theory. These are fundamental problems affecting every headline claim rather than omissions addressable by a small revision.
